html:
The Baymen were British woodcutters and former buccaneers who settled the coast of what is now Belize from the mid-1600s to cut logwood, a tree whose dye coloured European cloth.

Spain claimed the whole coast but never ruled it. The Treaty of Paris of 1763 and later treaties allowed the British to cut wood there without owning the land. From the late 1700s mahogany, cut deep in the forest by enslaved Africans brought through the Atlantic slave trade, replaced logwood as the main export.

The camps grew into Belize Town, and the settlement held off Spain at the Battle of St. George's Caye in 1798. This is why Belize became British and English-speaking, unlike its Spanish-speaking neighbours.
